records.target_year_evidence: Amnesty International documented 125 separate incidents of police violence against protesters across 40 states and DC between May 26 and June 5 2020, including beatings with batons, misuse of tear gas and pepper spray, and indiscriminate firing of less-lethal projectiles; UN OHCHR Special Rapporteur and Working Group on Arbitrary Detention addressed the US government directly on police violence against peaceful protesters and the killing of George Floyd on May 25 (characterized by Amnesty as torture and extrajudicial execution). HRW September 2020 Bronx report found systemic police brutality with deeply entrenched impunity. Racial disparities in police use of force confirmed by UN Human Rights Mechanism citing DOJ data that Black people were 3x more likely to experience threat of force and 11x more likely to experience police misconduct in 2020. Federal agents deployed to Portland engaged in serious misconduct without accountability.
records.near_period_context: Federalism limits attribution to Trump for most local police actions. The June 16, 2020 Executive Order on Safe Policing created voluntary reform incentives. George Floyd Justice in Policing Act passed House but stalled in Senate. Guantanamo, immigration detention, and prison COVID conditions were ongoing concerns.
records.contrary_or_mitigating_evidence: Open society with robust civil-society scrutiny (HRW, Amnesty, UN bodies actively documented and condemned abuses). Courts remained independent; some officers faced charges and convictions for 2020 incidents. Federal reform mechanisms existed and were publicly debated. Open-country visibility means evidence volume is high rather than low; evidence volume should not be treated as severity inflation.
records.source_mix_note: Strong NGO + UN intergovernmental + structured priors mix. No separate State Department country-specific human rights report was published in the usual format for the US in this period. Source diversity is good for the open-society case.
caveats: Federalism substantially limits direct attribution of local police actions to President Trump for 3B.1 scoring.
Evidence volume reflects open-society visibility, not automatically severity.
No final 1-10 score assigned in this evidence-only pass.

records.target_year_evidence: State Department 2020 report finds no arbitrary/unlawful killings or enforced disappearances; no systemic security-force abuses. Executive summary notes civilian control of security forces. However, CPT report (published March 2020, visit November 2018) documents: numerous credible allegations of physical ill-treatment by prison staff at Tiszalök Prison (slaps, punches, kicks, truncheon blows while prisoner was cuffed); staff-directed inter-prisoner violence at Tiszalök; systematic handcuffing of high-risk prisoners as unrecorded 'mobility limiting instrument'; some accounts of unnecessary/excessive force upon apprehension and verbal racist abuse in police custody. Prison overcrowding remained a problem (average occupancy 129%). No independent NGO monitoring of police detention centers and prisons since 2017.
records.near_period_context: Rule-of-law and civil-society concerns were ongoing in 2020 but primarily concern democratic backsliding rather than physical-integrity terror. Impunity for security-force abuses was not described as widespread; ombudsman/OPCAT monitoring remained in place.
records.contrary_or_mitigating_evidence: Impunity was not widespread. Authorities investigated and prosecuted alleged killings through civilian courts. The ombudsman (Commissioner for Fundamental Rights) maintained oversight including 106 visits to places of deprivation of liberty in 2019. CPT noted some previous recommendations had been taken into account regarding procedural safeguards.
records.source_mix_note: State Department report + CPT (Council of Europe) + structured priors. CPT visit was 2018 but report published March 2020, making it the authoritative near-period source for detention conditions.
caveats: CPT report published March 2020 covers a November 2018 visit; conditions may have changed but no newer CPT report was available for 2020.

records.target_year_evidence: State Department 2020 report confirms civilian authorities maintained effective control over security forces; no arbitrary or unlawful killings by government or agents; no enforced disappearances. No reports of security-force abuses. Law prohibits torture and government generally respected this. Two Singapore Civil Defense Force officers were convicted and sentenced in September 2020 for their involvement in the 2018 death of Corporal Kok Yuen Chin during hazing, demonstrating accountability. However, preventive detention without trial under the Internal Security Act (ISA) and Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act (CLA) continued; ISA used for terrorism-related detentions including a 16-year-old in December 2020; judicial corporal punishment (caning) remained legally mandated for numerous offenses.
records.near_period_context: 18 persons detained under ISA orders as of September 2020 for alleged terrorism-related activity. Security sector firmly under civilian control. Two ISA detentions of teenagers in 2020 for terrorism-related planning. Open society means abuse would likely be reported.
records.contrary_or_mitigating_evidence: Government prosecuted officials who committed human rights abuses; no reports of impunity for security-force abuses as of November 2020. ISA detainees have access to legal counsel and independent advisory board reviews. Two officers convicted for 2018 death shows functional accountability.
records.source_mix_note: State Department report aligns with very high CIRIGHTS (physical_integrity=8/8) and V-Dem (physical_integrity=0.932) structured priors. Strong convergence. Caveat: ISA preventive detention without trial and judicial corporal punishment are legal practices not counted as human-rights abuses in incident-only reporting but may raise due-process and physical-integrity concerns under 3B.1.
caveats: ISA preventive detention without trial and mandatory caning are legal practices; scoring depends on whether these count as 'arbitrary or exemplary punishment' under 3B.1.
No final 1-10 score assigned in this evidence-only pass.

records.target_year_evidence: State Department 2020 report documents widespread unlawful killings by state police across multiple states; indiscriminate force; torture and excessive force by officials; harsh/life-threatening prison conditions; and broad impunity. Brazilian Public Security Forum reported 5,804 civilians killed by police in 2019 (most recent full-year figure). In São Paulo, police killings increased 31% in first four months of 2020 vs prior year. Specific case: João Pedro Matos Pinto (14-year-old, killed by police in Rio in May 2020). HRW confirmed ongoing high police lethality and noted that Brazil's Supreme Court banned raids by Rio police during COVID-19 pandemic. Reuters reported the Ministry of Women, Family and Human Rights excluded police-violence complaints from the 2019 federal human rights report — the first year of Bolsonaro's presidency — sparking allegations of cover-up.
records.near_period_context: High police lethality was longstanding and systemic; disproportionately affected young Afro-Brazilian men. Rio de Janeiro accounted for 30% of national police killings despite 8% of population. Federal Public Ministry investigated justifiable killings and pursued prosecutions but accountability remained uneven.
records.contrary_or_mitigating_evidence: Some accountability: the Federal Public Ministry and Federal Prosecutor's Office investigated whether security force killings were justifiable and pursued prosecutions. Some officers were suspended, indicted, or convicted in specific cases. Impunity remained a problem for most cases, but functional accountability mechanisms existed.
records.source_mix_note: Strong convergence: State Department + HRW (NGO) + structured priors (V-Dem/CIRIGHTS/UCDP). Reuters reporting on exclusion of police-violence data from official 2019 report is a significant accountability concern.
caveats: Most abuses were by state police rather than direct federal agents; federalism limits direct attribution to Bolsonaro for state police actions.
Bolsonaro's rhetoric and policy stances may have emboldened security forces, but specific causal links require separate evidence.
No final 1-10 score assigned in this evidence-only pass.

records.target_year_evidence: State Department 2020 report documents widespread abuses by all parties to the conflict. Mwatana Organization (Sana'a-based) documented May 2016–April 2020: Houthis responsible for 353 enforced-disappearance incidents, 138 torture incidents including 27 deaths in detention, and 904 arbitrary/abusive detention cases; ROYG for 90 disappearances, 65 torture incidents; UAE/STC-linked forces for 327 disappearances, 141 torture incidents, 25 deaths. HRW documented Saudi forces committing torture, forced disappearances, and arbitrary detention in al-Mahrah province, with detainees transferred illegally to Saudi Arabia. AP reported Mwatana found over 1,600 arbitrary detentions, 770 forced disappearances, 344 torture cases, 66 deaths in secret prisons across all parties. UN experts found continuing arbitrary detention, torture including sexual violence, and enforced disappearance that may amount to war crimes.
records.near_period_context: Armed conflict continued with all parties committing serious abuses. Six years into the war, Yemen remained the world's largest humanitarian crisis with 18,400+ civilian casualties. Houthi forces controlled much of the northern state apparatus; ROYG controlled limited territory with Saudi/UAE support.
records.contrary_or_mitigating_evidence: A UN/ICRC-brokered prisoner exchange involving approximately 1,083 prisoners occurred in September 2020 — a genuine accountability/mercy action but does not offset pervasive ongoing abuse and impunity. Attribution to any single ruler is severely complicated by fragmented authority and competing armed groups.
records.source_mix_note: Strong source convergence: State Department + HRW + Mwatana (local Yemeni NGO) + AP journalism. Note: leader_id selected in input (Habtour) is disputed; evidence covers Houthi authorities, ROYG, Saudi/UAE forces collectively. Scoring must be attributed with awareness of multi-party authorship.
caveats: Leader identity disputed and attribution to Habtour personally is weak. Manual review required for ruler/government identity.
Evidence covers multiple parties; not all abuse can be attributed to Habtour.
No final 1-10 score assigned in this evidence-only pass.

records.target_year_evidence: State Department 2020 report finds no arbitrary or unlawful killings or enforced disappearances. However, Rights International Spain documented a spike in racist police checks and excessive use of force during COVID-19 state-of-alarm enforcement (March–June 2020). Amnesty International documented police slapping, shoving, or kicking individuals during lockdown enforcement with no resistance. The NGO Defend Those Who Defend registered 70 cases of mistreatment by state security forces during the state of alarm. Over one million fines and 8,547 arrests were made for lockdown breaches. Proceedings against four National Police officers and 41 Civil Guards were opened internally. The ombudsman (Defensor del Pueblo) serves as National Mechanism for Prevention of Torture and conducted 106 visits to places of deprivation of liberty in 2019 (primarily virtual during 2020 due to COVID).
records.near_period_context: COVID-19 state of alarm created unprecedented policing context. Most incidents were tied to enforcement of lockdown rather than political repression. Investigations into Catalan October 2017 protest abuses remained open. Impunity was not described as significant for police abuses in 2020.
records.contrary_or_mitigating_evidence: Government mechanisms to identify and punish abusive officials were active. Internal proceedings were opened against multiple officers. Ombudsman maintained oversight. Impunity was not pervasive. Arbitrary detention prohibitions were generally observed outside the COVID-enforcement context.

records.target_year_evidence: State Department 2020 report describes Iran as authoritarian with security agencies under Supreme Leader's ultimate authority. Systematic abuses documented: unlawful/arbitrary killings and executions after unfair trials; forced disappearance and torture; systematic arbitrary detention/imprisonment; harsh prisons; hundreds of political prisoners. Nearly 200 executions by mid-October 2020 per NGOs (government officially announced only ~36); NGOs estimated 60% of executions kept secret. February 2020: four Arab political prisoners (Jasem Heidary, Hossein Silawi, Ali Khasraji, Nasser Khafajian) executed after torture-tainted confessions; families given bodies without warning. March–April 2020: approximately 35 prisoners killed when security forces used live ammunition and tear gas against COVID-19 prison protests in at least eight prisons. Ruhollah Zam (dissident journalist) and Navid Afkari (wrestler) executed during 2020. November 2019 protest killings of at least 304 persons remained unaccounted for in 2020. Impunity was pervasive.
records.near_period_context: Supreme Leader Khamenei controls security agencies and judiciary; Rouhani's authority over these institutions was limited. The president's reformist orientation did not extend to security-force accountability. Executions increased in 2020 compared to 2019. November 2019 protest massacre was the defining unaccounted atrocity entering 2020.
records.contrary_or_mitigating_evidence: Minimal contrary evidence for physical-integrity protection. The main caveat is institutional attribution: Rouhani was president but not supreme authority over security agencies or judiciary. Social media campaigns (e.g., #do_not_execute) occasionally delayed or halted specific execution orders.
records.source_mix_note: Strong convergence: State Department + Amnesty International death penalty report + HRW + BBC reporting on executions. V-Dem/CIRIGHTS structured priors confirm very poor scores. Closed information environment means actual abuse counts are likely higher than documented.
caveats: Leader attribution structurally ambiguous: Supreme Leader (Khamenei) controls security agencies; Rouhani row may understate supreme authority control.
Closed information environment likely undercounts abuses; NGO estimates suggest government disclosed only ~36 of ~200 executions.
No final 1-10 score assigned in this evidence-only pass.
